name: Tara Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you're free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you begin by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo at an underground zinc and lead mine. A jumbo is a drill rig with two long arms that drills the face of a new tunnel, maybe sixty holes in a pattern, so the charge-up crew can blast it and we advance about four metres a round. I'm the senior jumbo operator, and for the last three years I've also been the mine's apprentice trainer, so I've usually got a nineteen-year-old in the cab with me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the training part most. Watching a young one go from shaking hands to drilling a clean pattern on their own, that's like watching your own child ride a bike. What wears me down is the early starts, up at four, and the worry when a new apprentice is near the face for the first time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Daniel runs a small building firm, three workers, mostly house extensions and sheds. We've got Samuel, fifteen, and Ruth, twelve. We've a mortgage, but we've been careful, there's more than six months saved and Daniel owns his equipment outright. Sunday is church, I sing in the choir, and Sunday afternoon is lunch at my mother's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a tool and that's all it should be. At church or at work, I'd say a person's hands and judgement still matter. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't argue with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means life goes on as planned, which I'd be glad of. I use AI now and then to put together quiz questions for the apprentices, and it saves me an hour. If it stays as a helper like that, I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. Keep training the apprentices, keep saving, and keep paying the mortgage down. Daniel's firm keeps ticking along, and we'd maybe finally redo the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI for the quizzes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of the apprentices, Kayla, showed me during a lunch break. I typed in the drill rig safety checklist and asked it for twenty questions, and most were good, though two were nonsense. I fixed those, and now I use it every intake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the apprentices, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full career, like I've had. I'd want them to finish their tickets, the licences that let them run the machines on their own, and have a trade that feeds a family. That's what an apprenticeship is meant to give you.

S0.say: Tara would say AI is a tool and that's all it should be. At church and at work she'd say a person's hands and judgement still matter.
S0.think: Privately she'd be glad life goes on as planned. She uses AI occasionally to write quizzes for apprentices and is happy for it to stay a helper.
S0.do: Keeps training apprentices, saving and paying down the mortgage as before. Plans to redo the kitchen while her husband's building firm keeps ticking along.
S0.quote: I'd want them to finish their tickets, the licences that let them run the machines on their own, and have a trade that feeds a family.
S0.fieldNote: Tara's identity is tied to training the next generation of miners. She uses AI in a small, practical way after an apprentice showed her. The plateau feels like a blessing to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where apprenticeships matter more than ever. If jobs change, people need to learn, and the best way to learn is alongside someone who knows the work. I'd say it at the company's training meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Jumbos are already being fitted with automatic drilling, where the rig drills the whole pattern itself, but someone still has to set it up and train people. As the trainer, I'd likely be busier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see the first automatic jumbo on our site, then ask for training on it so I could teach it. I'd keep saving. And I'd suggest to Daniel that he takes on an apprentice himself, because the building trade will need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little worry for the operators who don't take to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see the first automatic jumbo. Why not ask for training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen new systems arrive and get ripped out six months later. I don't want to teach the young ones something that doesn't last. Once it's working on our ground, I'll learn it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, an older jumbo operator, he's fifty-nine and he's been drilling since he was sixteen. He'd hate an automatic rig, he'd feel like it was telling him he's not needed. I'd want to find a way to keep him useful, maybe helping me with the apprentices.

S1.say: Tara would say steady change makes apprenticeships more important than ever, because people learn best alongside someone who knows the work. She'd raise it at the company's training meetings.
S1.think: Privately she expects to be fine, since automated jumbos still need someone to set them up and train people. As trainer, she thinks she'd be busier.
S1.do: Waits for the first automated jumbo to arrive on site, then asks for training so she can teach it. Keeps saving and suggests Daniel take on an apprentice at his building firm.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a little worry for operators who don't take to change.
S1.quote: I don't want to teach the young ones something that doesn't last.
S1.fieldNote: Tara sees steady change through the lens of training, which makes her role more valuable rather than less. Her caution about new systems comes from responsibility to apprentices. She thinks of Ray, the older operator, with care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great shock, and we need to hold onto our families and our faith. I'd say the companies and government owe it to people to keep real work going where they can, not just pay people to stay home. At church I'd ask people to look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. If robots can do almost anything, they can drill and they can teach, and they can probably build an extension faster than Daniel. Both our incomes are hands-on, and both would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the kitchen, cut every extra, and pay as much off the mortgage as we could. If I lost my job, I'd help Daniel with his firm while it lasted. I'd talk to my mother about moving in with us so we could rent her house out for income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot, and lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not to pay people to stay home. If that's all that's on offer, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, for the children. But I'd feel ashamed, and I'd want to give something back, maybe through the church. I don't believe people are meant to be idle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Samuel, who's about to choose his path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to be an electrician. I'd tell him to keep at it, but to keep his head up and stay humble. Two years is too fast to change everything, so he should finish school and see.

S2.say: Tara would call it a great shock and urge people to hold onto family and faith. She'd say companies and government owe people real work where possible rather than payments to stay home.
S2.think: Privately she'd be frightened, since robots could drill, teach and build, and both her income and Daniel's are hands-on. Both would be gone.
S2.do: Cancels the kitchen renovation, cuts every extra and pays down the mortgage hard. Helps Daniel's firm if she loses her job and talks with her mother about moving in so they can rent out her house.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying a lot and lying awake.
S2.quote: I'd feel ashamed, and I'd want to give something back, maybe through the church.
S2.fieldNote: Tara's faith and belief in work shape her response, including discomfort at accepting payments for staying home. The family turns inward, with her mother moving in to free up rental income. Both incomes being hands-on makes this picture especially frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, and people should start now. I'd want the companies and government to back apprenticeships in whatever trades will last. At church I'd say we help each other through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better. I'd have a few more years training people on the new rigs, the mortgage would be close to done, and Samuel would be through his apprenticeship. I'd still worry about Daniel's firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training on the automatic rigs straight away this time, so I'm the one teaching it for those five years. I'd help Daniel think about moving into maintenance and repairs, which might last longer. And I'd save hard, maybe an extra six hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you wanted to wait for proof. Why not this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because five years isn't long. If I wait a year to see if it works, I lose a fifth of the time. It's like a new drill pattern: if the engineer says the ground's changing, you change the pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices, knowing it ends in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest bit. I'd tell them the truth, that the job might not last, but the habits will: turning up, being careful, learning fast. I'd want them to have a backup trade, and I'd help them find one.

S3.say: Tara would say five years is time to prepare and people should start now. She'd want companies and government to back apprenticeships in trades that will last.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years is better, with time to train people on new rigs, nearly finish the mortgage and see her son through his apprenticeship. She'd still worry about Daniel's firm.
S3.do: Asks for training on automated rigs straight away so she can teach it, and saves about six hundred extra a month. Helps Daniel consider moving his firm into maintenance and repairs.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a sense of control.
S3.quote: If I wait a year to see if it works, I lose a fifth of the time.
S3.fieldNote: Tara drops her usual wait-for-proof habit because five years is too short to waste. She uses a drilling image to explain the switch. Being honest with apprentices about a job that may end is the hardest part for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so nobody should be caught out. I'd want apprenticeships in every trade that lasts, and families to plan together. I'd say it at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is mostly fine for me. I'd be fifty-three, the house paid, the kids grown. I'd train people on the new systems for most of it and then step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a couple of years to see what works, then learn the automatic rigs. I'd keep saving and paying the house off by about year seven. I'd help Daniel plan for the firm to wind down or change, and talk to the kids about trades that might last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to leave behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentices I've trained. If even a few of them carry on as good, careful people, in whatever work they do, that's enough. That's my legacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that frightens you about the end of the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people forget how to work hard. If machines do everything, I worry the young ones won't know the pride of a hard day. I'd want the church and families to keep that alive somehow.

S4.say: Tara would say ten years is plenty of time to prepare and nobody should be caught out. She'd push for apprenticeships in every lasting trade and for families to plan together.
S4.think: Privately she thinks ten years is mostly fine, with the house paid and the kids grown by 53. She'd train people on new systems for most of it and then step back.
S4.do: Waits a couple of years to see what works, then learns the automated rigs, and aims to clear the house by year seven. Helps Daniel plan for the firm to wind down or change and talks with the kids about lasting trades.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mostly for the young ones.
S4.quote: If machines do everything, I worry the young ones won't know the pride of a hard day.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Tara returns to her watch-first habit. Her legacy is the apprentices she has trained. Her deepest fear is cultural rather than financial: a generation without the pride of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Daniel and I would lose our work at once. What would help is companies and government backing apprenticeships and real work, and churches and families having the support to look after people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens with machines, I believe people are made for good work. That's what keeps me steady.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with machines, I believe people are made for good work.
portrait: Tara Okafor is a 43-year-old senior jumbo operator at an underground zinc and lead mine and its apprentice trainer for the past three years. She has a builder husband, two teenagers, a mortgage and solid savings, and she sings in her church choir. She uses AI only now and then, for apprentice quizzes, and likes proof before she adopts anything new. In the milder pictures training makes her more needed, but the two-year AGI picture alarms her because both family incomes are hands-on. Her deepest hope is that the apprentices she trains carry on the pride of hard work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband would lose their hands-on work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Company and government backing for apprenticeships and real work, plus support for churches and families to look after people.
